meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Any Time You See Anything Big and Working Well, You Want To Take It Over'?
meta.ogDescription: The Churchill lavatory joke: verdicted apocryphal by the standard Churchill compendium, and first evidenced third-hand in a 1958 letter.

answer.label: Not Churchill — apocryphal, and the wording is from a 1965 memoir
answer.authorDates: Credited to Winston Churchill (1874–1965) · verdict of the standard Churchill compendium: apocryphal
answer.sourceLine: This is the House of Commons lavatory story — Churchill declining to stand next to a Labour politician because socialists nationalise anything big and in good working order. Richard Langworth, who compiled Churchill By Himself, places it in his appendix of “Red Herrings: False Attributions” and rules it “Apocryphal Churchill”. Quote Investigator ↗ finds the earliest trace in a private letter of 22 December 1958 — roughly a decade after the conversation is supposed to have happened, and reaching the writer through at least three intermediaries. This exact wording is later still.
answer.confidenceText: Disputed — no contemporary record, a third-hand first sighting, and a shifting cast of characters.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: None contemporary. No record of the exchange from the 1940s, when it is said to have happened.
A letter from Dean Acheson to Felix Frankfurter, 22 December 1958 — the story relayed via Scotty Reston and Stewart Alsop, who had it from Hubert Humphrey

source.excerpt: One time Shinwell was in the men’s room of the House of Commons when Churchill entered. There was no one else there, but Churchill walked right by Shinwell to the farthest end. “I say, Winnie,” said Shinwell, “I hope there’s nothing personal between us.” And Churchill replied, “I don’t take chances, Mannie. I know you. Any time you see anything big and working well, you want to take it over.”
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ reports that the earliest evidence it located is a letter of 22 December 1958 from Dean Acheson to Felix Frankfurter, and that Acheson “did not hear the story directly from either of the participants” — it came via the journalists Scotty Reston and Stewart Alsop, who were relaying a version told by Hubert Humphrey. That letter is printed in Among Friends: Personal Letters of Dean Acheson ↗ (1980), p. 153.

In Acheson’s version the punchline is different and more parliamentary: “whenever you see a means of production in good working order you want to nationalize it.” The compressed modern line — “anything big and working well” — does not appear until Harry Bannister’s 1965 memoir, which also changes who Churchill is talking to.

The cast keeps moving, which is the classic signature of an anecdote rather than a record. QI documents Shinwell in 1965, Attlee in a 1979 trade journal, a cigar and no lavatory at all in a 1980 Citibank newsletter, and Attlee again in William Manchester’s The Last Lion ↗ (1983) — where Manchester’s own footnote says the story was told to him by Sir David Pitblado in 1980.

The Churchill quotation literature does not accept it. Langworth’s Churchill By Himself lists it among false attributions, dates the alleged remark to “circa 1948”, notes it is “recorded by Manchester and others, but not attributed”, and gives the verdict “Apocryphal Churchill”. QI’s own conclusion is that “the evidentiary support is not strong” and the tale “may have been constructed or embellished by a humorist”.
source.cutTag: Harry Bannister, The Education of a Broadcaster (1965)
source.excerptNote: That is the earliest appearance of the sentence in this form, and it is worth noticing who is in it. Bannister, an American broadcasting executive, casts the Labour politician Emanuel Shinwell, not Clement Attlee — and the story reaches the reader with no source at all. Later tellings swap Attlee back in, move the joke to the bar, replace the urinal with a cigar, and steadily tighten the punchline.

source.rightsNote: We assert no rights status. The words have no established author: the sentence is an anecdote whose speaker is disputed, whose wording changes with every retelling, and whose earliest printing — a 1965 memoir — presents it as reported speech with no source. There is no work to attach a first-publication date to, so we do not claim one.

author.name: Winston Churchill
author.heading: About Winston Churchill
author.metaLine: 1874–1965 · British prime minister, author and Nobel laureate in Literature
author.bio: Churchill is the most quotable politician in the English language and, partly for that reason, one of the most falsely quoted — the standard compilation of his words needs a whole appendix for lines he never said. He genuinely was a formidable and often coarse wit, and he genuinely did spend the late 1940s attacking Labour’s nationalisation programme, which is exactly why a joke combining the two travels so easily under his name without anyone asking for a source.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: Almost every element of this story has been swapped out at some point except Churchill himself, and even he is not securely in it.

items.why: Richard Langworth’s Churchill By Himself, the standard compilation of Churchill’s words, files this among “Red Herrings: False Attributions” and returns the verdict “Apocryphal Churchill”. There is no contemporary record of the exchange, and the first trace of it is a private letter written about a decade later.

The earliest version, in Dean Acheson’s 1958 letter, names Attlee. The earliest version carrying this wording, Harry Bannister’s 1965 memoir, names Shinwell. Later tellings mostly revert to Attlee. A real exchange does not usually change one of its two participants.

items.who: The Commons lavatory — or the bar
items.why: The 1980 Citibank version relocates the joke to the bar of the Commons and replaces the urinal with a cigar Churchill hides in his breast pocket, prefacing the whole thing with the word “apocryphal”. QI collects all the variants ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: It is a good joke about nationalisation that has been in circulation since at least 1958 and has never been tied to Churchill by anyone who heard him say it.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: The joke only works in a specific decade. Attlee’s 1945 government took the coal mines, the railways, electricity, gas, road haulage and the Bank of England into public ownership, and Churchill spent those years in opposition attacking exactly that programme. A gag about socialists nationalising anything large and functional was, in the late 1940s, straightforward political commentary with a lavatory attached.

That plausibility is also the problem. The story is so well-fitted to its moment, and so exactly the sort of thing Churchill is imagined saying, that it needs no evidence to spread — which is roughly the definition of an apocryphal quotation.
detailsBody: Follow the wording rather than the plot and the drift is easy to see. Acheson’s 1958 letter has Churchill say: “whenever you see a means of production in good working order you want to nationalize it” — a clumsy sentence with a textbook phrase in the middle of it. By 1965 it has become “any time you see anything big and working well, you want to take it over”. By 1983, in Manchester, it is down to nine words: “Every time you see something big, you want to nationalize it.” Anecdotes get funnier as they travel; transcripts do not.

The 1958 letter is also worth reading for what Acheson does not claim. He is passing on a story he heard from two journalists, who had it from another politician, who attributed it to Attlee. Nobody in that chain was in the room, and the room is supposed to have been a lavatory a decade earlier.

There is one honest argument on the other side, and QI makes it: a joke of this kind may have been considered unprintable in the 1940s and circulated by word of mouth for years before anyone wrote it down. That would explain a late first sighting. It would not explain the migrating participants, and it is not evidence — which is why the verdict stays at apocryphal rather than unproven-but-likely.
context.pull: A story this well-fitted to its moment does not need evidence to spread. That is the problem with it.

sourcesVerified.claim: The earliest evidence QI located is a letter dated 22 December 1958 from Dean Acheson to Felix Frankfurter, in which Acheson relays the story second-hand via Scotty Reston and Stewart Alsop, who had it from Hubert Humphrey.
In Acheson's 1958 version the punchline reads 'whenever you see a means of production in good working order you want to nationalize it', and the other participant is Clement Attlee.

The exact wording 'Any time you see anything big and working well, you want to take it over' first appears in Harry Bannister's The Education of a Broadcaster (Simon and Schuster, 1965), page 279, where the other participant is Emanuel Shinwell, not Attlee.

Richard M. Langworth's Churchill By Himself places the anecdote in an appendix titled 'Red Herrings: False Attributions', dates the alleged remark circa 1948, notes it is recorded by Manchester and others but not attributed, and gives the verdict 'Apocryphal Churchill'.
William Manchester's The Last Lion (1983) carries the anecdote with Attlee, and Manchester's footnote states the story was told to him by Sir David Pitblado in 1980.
A 1980 Citibank Monthly Economic Letter printed a version set in the bar of the Commons involving a cigar, and explicitly labelled the tale apocryphal.
QI concludes that the evidentiary support is not strong and that the tale may have been constructed or embellished by a humorist.
